```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)
```

### Problem 1
```{r load_noaa}
# Load the New York NOAA weather dataset
data("ny_noaa")

ny_noaa
```
```{r inspect_noaa}
# Check dataset size, structure, and missing values
dim(ny_noaa)

glimpse(ny_noaa)

ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    missing_prcp = sum(is.na(prcp)),
    missing_snow = sum(is.na(snow)),
    missing_snwd = sum(is.na(snwd)),
    missing_tmax = sum(is.na(tmax)),
    missing_tmin = sum(is.na(tmin))
  )
```
```{r clean_noaa}
# Clean dates and weather measurements
noaa_clean =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(format(date, "%Y")),
    month = as.integer(format(date, "%m")),
    day = as.integer(format(date, "%d")),
    prcp = prcp / 10,
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
  )

noaa_clean

```
```{r check_noaa_clean}
# Check cleaned variables
noaa_clean |>
  select(date, year, month, day, prcp, snow, snwd, tmax, tmin) |>
  head()
```
```{r snowfall_frequency}
# Find the most common snowfall values
snowfall_frequency =
  noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE)

snowfall_frequency |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```
```{r missing_noaa}
# Calculate percent missing for key weather variables
noaa_clean |>
  summarize(
    prcp_missing = mean(is.na(prcp)) * 100,
    snow_missing = mean(is.na(snow)) * 100,
    snwd_missing = mean(is.na(snwd)) * 100,
    tmax_missing = mean(is.na(tmax)) * 100,
    tmin_missing = mean(is.na(tmin)) * 100
  )
```
The original `ny_noaa` dataset contains 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables. Each row represents a daily weather observation for a station identified by `id` and `date`. Key weather variables include precipitation (`prcp`), snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), maximum temperature (`tmax`), and minimum temperature (`tmin`). Missing data are fairly common for some variables: about 5.6% of precipitation values, 14.7% of snowfall values, 22.8% of snow depth values, and 43.7% of maximum temperature values are missing.

The most common snowfall value is 0 mm, with 2,008,508 observations. Other common values include 25, 13, 51, and 76 mm. Zero is by far the most common because most station-days do not have snowfall. The other repeated values likely reflect common snowfall amounts originally recorded in inches and converted to millimeters.

```{r jan_july_summary}
# Calculate average max temperature by station and year
jan_july_df =
  noaa_clean |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(is.finite(mean_tmax))

jan_july_df

```
```{r jan_july_plot}
# Plot average max temperature in January and July
jan_july_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = mean_tmax,
      group = id
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.25) +
  facet_wrap(~month, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature by Station",
    subtitle = "January and July across years",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average maximum temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```
```{r tmax_tmin_plot}
# Show the relationship between maximum and minimum temperature
temp_plot =
  noaa_clean |>
  filter(
    !is.na(tmax),
    !is.na(tmin)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin_2d(bins = 50) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs. Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

temp_plot

```
Average maximum temperatures are much lower in January than in July across stations. Both months show noticeable year-to-year variation, but there is no strong long-term pattern that is obvious across the full period. Most station averages cluster fairly closely together, although there are a few unusually low station-year averages in both January and July that stand out from the rest.

```{r snowfall_plot}
# Show snowfall distributions by year
snow_plot =
  noaa_clean |>
  filter(
    snow > 0,
    snow < 100
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    breaks = as.character(seq(1981, 2010, by = 5))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

snow_plot
```
```{r combined_weather_plot, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}
# Combine temperature and snowfall plots
temp_plot + snow_plot +
  plot_layout(ncol = 2) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Temperature and Snowfall Patterns in New York"
  )

```
Maximum and minimum temperatures have a strong positive relationship, with most observations concentrated along a clear upward pattern. There are also a small number of unusually extreme temperature observations outside the main concentration. Snowfall distributions are fairly similar across years, with most nonzero snowfall measurements concentrated at lower values. Some years have more high snowfall observations near the upper end of the restricted range, but there is not a clear long-term shift in the overall distribution.



# Problem 2

```{r clean_nhanes_covar}
# Import and clean demographic data
nhanes_covar =
  read_csv(
    "./data/nhanes_covar.csv",
    skip = 4,
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    sex = case_match(
      sex,
      1 ~ "Male",
      2 ~ "Female"
    ),
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = case_match(
      education,
      1 ~ "Less than high school",
      2 ~ "High school equivalent",
      3 ~ "More than high school"
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  )

nhanes_covar

```
```{r load_nhanes_accel}
# Import accelerometer data
nhanes_accel =
  read_csv(
    "./data/nhanes_accel.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

nhanes_accel

```

```{r merge_nhanes}
# Merge demographic and accelerometer data
nhanes_df =
  inner_join(
    nhanes_covar,
    nhanes_accel,
    by = "seqn"
  )

dim(nhanes_df)

glimpse(nhanes_df)

```



```{r nhanes_table}
# Count participants by education and sex
education_sex_table =
  nhanes_df |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  )

knitr::kable(
  education_sex_table,
  caption = "Number of Participants by Education Level and Sex"
)

```
```{r age_distribution}
# Compare age distributions by sex and education
nhanes_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = age,
      fill = sex
    )
  ) +
  geom_density(
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~education, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education Level",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```
Participant counts are fairly balanced by sex among those with less than a high school education and those with more than a high school education. In the high school equivalent group, there are more men than women (35 compared with 23). The more than high school group contains the largest number of participants overall.

The age distributions vary across education level and sex. Among participants with more than a high school education, women are more concentrated at younger ages, while men are spread more broadly across the age range. The other education groups show substantial overlap between men and women, although the shapes of their age distributions differ somewhat.

```{r total_activity}
# Calculate total daily activity for each participant
nhanes_total =
  nhanes_df |>
  mutate(
    total_activity = rowSums(
      across(min1:min1440),
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )

nhanes_total |>
  select(
    seqn,
    sex,
    age,
    education,
    total_activity
  ) |>
  head()

```

```{r total_activity_plot}
# Plot total daily activity against age
nhanes_total |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = age,
      y = total_activity,
      color = sex
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(
    se = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~education, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total daily activity",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```





Total daily activity generally decreases with age, although the pattern differs across education levels and between men and women. The decline is especially noticeable among participants with less than a high school education. There is substantial variation among individuals at similar ages, and the smoothed trends suggest that the relationship between age and activity is not completely linear.

```{r tidy_activity}
# Reshape minute-level activity data
nhanes_long =
  nhanes_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "activity"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = parse_number(minute),
    hour = (minute - 1) / 60
  )

nhanes_long |>
  select(
    seqn,
    sex,
    age,
    education,
    minute,
    hour,
    activity
  ) |>
  head()

```
```{r activity_timecourse}
# Calculate average activity throughout the day
activity_summary =
  nhanes_long |>
  group_by(
    education,
    sex,
    minute,
    hour
  ) |>
  summarize(
    mean_activity = mean(activity, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Plot 24-hour activity patterns
activity_summary |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = hour,
      y = mean_activity,
      color = sex
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_smooth(
    se = FALSE,
    span = 0.1
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~education,
    nrow = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 4)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity Patterns by Education Level",
    x = "Hour of day",
    y = "Mean activity",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```
Activity is lowest overnight, rises sharply in the morning, remains relatively high through much of the day, and then declines later in the evening. The overall daily pattern is similar across education groups. Women generally show somewhat higher daytime activity than men in the high school equivalent and more than high school groups, while the difference between men and women is smaller among participants with less than a high school education.

# Problem 3

```{r load_citibike}
# Import Citi Bike data
citi_jan_2020 =
  read_csv(
    "./data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "January"
  )

citi_july_2020 =
  read_csv(
    "./data/July 2020 Citi.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "July"
  )

citi_jan_2024 =
  read_csv(
    "./data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "January"
  )

citi_july_2024 =
  read_csv(
    "./data/July 2024 Citi.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "July"
  )

```

```{r combine_citibike}
# Combine Citi Bike datasets
citi_df =
  bind_rows(
    citi_jan_2020,
    citi_july_2020,
    citi_jan_2024,
    citi_july_2024
  ) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c("January", "July")
    )
  )

dim(citi_df)

glimpse(citi_df)

```
```{r clean_citibike}
# Clean Citi Bike variables
citi_df =
  citi_df |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(
      year,
      levels = c(2020, 2024)
    ),
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c("January", "July")
    ),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual,
      levels = c("casual", "member"),
      labels = c("Casual", "Member")
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(rideable_type),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday",
        "Tuesday",
        "Wednesday",
        "Thursday",
        "Friday",
        "Saturday",
        "Sunday"
      )
    )
  )

glimpse(citi_df)

```
The combined Citi Bike dataset contains 99,485 rides and 9 variables. Each row represents one ride and includes the bike type, day of the week, ride duration, starting and ending station, membership status, year, and month. The data include rides from January and July in both 2020 and 2024, allowing comparisons over time, season, membership status, and bike type.

```{r ride_count_table}
# Count rides by year, month, and membership status
ride_count_table =
  citi_df |>
  count(
    year,
    month,
    member_casual,
    name = "rides"
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = rides,
    values_fill = 0
  )

knitr::kable(
  ride_count_table,
  caption = "Number of Citi Bike Rides by Year, Month, and Membership Status"
)

```
Ride counts are higher in July than in January in both years, and members account for more rides than casual riders in every year-month combination. Ridership also increased substantially from 2020 to 2024. The largest number of rides occurred in July 2024, with 36,262 member rides and 10,894 casual rides.
```{r popular_stations}
# Find the most popular starting stations in July 2024
popular_stations =
  citi_df |>
  filter(
    year == "2024",
    month == "July"
  ) |>
  count(
    start_station_name,
    sort = TRUE,
    name = "rides"
  ) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

knitr::kable(
  popular_stations,
  caption = "Five Most Popular Starting Stations in July 2024"
)

```
The five most popular starting stations in July 2024 were Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers, University Pl & E 14 St, W 21 St & 6 Ave, West St & Chambers St, and W 31 St & 7 Ave. Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers had the most rides, with 163 rides originating there.

```{r median_duration_plot}
# Calculate median ride duration by weekday, month, and year
median_duration =
  citi_df |>
  group_by(
    year,
    month,
    weekdays
  ) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(
      duration,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Plot median ride duration
median_duration |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = weekdays,
      y = median_duration,
      color = month,
      group = month
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~year) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Citi Bike Ride Duration by Day of Week",
    x = "Day of week",
    y = "Median ride duration (minutes)",
    color = "Month"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )

```
Median ride duration is consistently longer in July than in January in both years. Ride durations were also generally longer in 2020 than in 2024. The difference between January and July is especially pronounced in 2020, and July 2020 shows a noticeable increase in median duration on the weekend. In 2024, ride durations vary less across the days of the week.


```{r ride_distribution_2024}
# Compare 2024 ride duration distributions
citi_df |>
  filter(year == "2024") |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = duration,
      fill = rideable_type
    )
  ) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_grid(
    member_casual ~ month
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(0, 60)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride Duration Distributions in 2024",
    subtitle = "By month, membership status, and bike type",
    x = "Ride duration (minutes)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Bike type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```
In 2024, casual riders generally have broader ride-duration distributions and longer right tails than members, indicating more longer-duration rides. Member rides are more concentrated at shorter durations in both January and July. Differences between classic and electric bikes are smaller than the differences by membership status, although electric-bike rides tend to be somewhat more concentrated at shorter durations, particularly among casual riders.
